item.title: Beyond the Drone: How XAG Is Betting on Autonomous Farming
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s Note: There is no shortage of technology news, yet many promising Chinese startups still remain largely unknown to global audiences. At the same time, the constant flow of funding news, product launches, and new technologies makes it harder to see which companies truly deserve attention. DragonLab is TechNode’s effort to close that gap, looking […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: There is no shortage of technology news, yet many promising Chinese startups still remain largely unknown to global audiences. At the same time, the constant flow of funding news, product launches, and new technologies makes it harder to see which companies truly deserve attention. DragonLab is TechNode’s effort to close that gap, looking past the noise to discover China’s next wave of innovation—emerging companies, ambitious founders, and breakthrough technologies that have yet to receive global attention.

The agricultural drone is no longer the hard part. XAG is now trying to automate the charging, refilling and ground work that still keep people in the loop.

What does an automated farm look like? A tractor moving through a field without a driver? A drone spraying crops without a pilot? Or a system where machines can finish a job, recharge, refill and start again with little human intervention?

All three visions are beginning to take shape. In the U.S., John Deere has brought autonomy to tractors and precision spraying through products such as its autonomous 8R tractor and camera-based See & Spray technology. Texas-based Hylio has taken another route, building autonomous agricultural drones and software that lets one operator manage multiple aircraft.

China’s XAG overlaps with both approaches but is trying to connect more pieces of farm automation. Its portfolio spans agricultural drones, ground robots, autopilot systems for conventional machinery and smart-farm infrastructure. Its newest products push that strategy one step further: automating some of the work that happens when a drone is back on the ground.

At XAG’s SuperX Farm in Guangzhou on July 6, founder Peng Bin used a mobile app to send two X150 agricultural drones into the field. More notable was what happened between flights. An XA1 drone station recharged the aircraft, while an LM1 system mixed and refilled liquid for spraying. The process from charging and refilling to takeoff took about three minutes.

The setup forms XAG’s new X Series agricultural robot system, combining an X100 or X150 drone with a drone station and automated liquid-handling equipment to automate route planning, spraying, charging, refilling, and cleaning.

The harder part starts when the drone lands. Charging, refilling, cleaning, and relaunching still require human hands. XAG’s latest system is designed to automate more of that turnaround.

A long pivot into agriculture

XAG began in Guangzhou in 2007 as XAircraft. Before settling on farming, the company experimented with power-line inspection, search and rescue, logistics and other drone applications.

Its agricultural turn came in 2013. During a trip to cotton fields in Xinjiang, the team began considering whether drones could replace labor-intensive pesticide spraying, co-founder Gong Jiaqin said in a 2022 interview with TechNode. XAG first developed the business in Xinjiang, expanded across China and began moving overseas around 2017 and 2018.

Japan became one of its first major overseas markets. Gong told TechNode that its fragmented farmland resembled China’s more closely than the large farms common in countries such as the U.S., Australia and Brazil. An aging rural population also created demand for smaller automated machines.

Internationalization was slow by design. Hardware had to meet different certification requirements, while farmers often needed one or more planting seasons to decide whether new equipment could genuinely improve productivity. Gong said the company’s early years overseas were therefore spent largely on product validation and local partnerships.

Capital followed the expansion. In 2020, XAG raised RMB 1.2 billion, or roughly $182 million at the time, in a round co-led by Baidu Capital and SoftBank Vision Fund II. GL Ventures invested another RMB 300 million in 2021.

XAG withdrew its STAR Market application in 2022, when the company was still loss-making and China’s capital markets were under pressure. A person familiar with XAG told 21st Century Business Herald at the time that market conditions were the main consideration behind the withdrawal.

When XAG returned to the public markets with a Hong Kong listing application several years later, its finances looked markedly different. Revenue rose from RMB 614.5 million in 2023 to RMB 1.07 billion in 2024 and RMB 1.17 billion in 2025, while the company swung from a RMB 132.8 million loss to a RMB 123.8 million profit over the same period.

The turnaround was driven largely by rising overseas drone sales, higher gross margins and tighter expense ratios.

XAG later withdrew its application for Shanghai’s STAR Market in 2022 and turned to Hong Kong. Its latest Hong Kong listing filing shows revenue rising from RMB 614.5 million in 2023 to RMB 1.07 billion in 2024 and RMB 1.17 billion in 2025. Net profit reached RMB 123.8 million in 2025.

From an autonomous drone to an autonomous workflow

XAG’s 2026 lineup extends beyond drones. It includes the P200, P150 Ultra and P120 agricultural drones, along with agricultural rovers, autopilot systems for conventional machinery, smart irrigation products, and the new RM80 autonomous mower.

The X Series offers the clearest indication of where the company wants to go next.

The X100 carries a 50-liter liquid tank, while the X150 carries 85 liters. Rather than requiring workers to handle every turnaround manually, the drone can return to an XA1 station for charging, while the LM1 system prepares and replenishes spraying liquid. The system can also automatically clean the tank, pipelines, and nozzles after a job.

The RM80, introduced at the same July event, extends the automation push to the ground. The electric four-wheel-drive machine can plan routes, automatically return and perform mowing and vegetation-clearing tasks in orchards and fields.

Compared with U.S. companies, XAG’s distinction lies partly in the breadth of the system it is assembling.

Texas-based Hylio focuses on aerial application, with software that lets one operator manage multiple agricultural drones. John Deere approaches automation through farm machinery, using autonomous tractors and camera-based See & Spray systems for targeted weed control.

XAG sits somewhere across those categories. It sells aerial spraying systems like Hylio, but has also developed ground robots, tractor autopilot and farm IoT products. The X Series adds another layer by automating charging and chemical handling around the drone itself.

That breadth, however, has not yet translated into equally diversified revenue. Agricultural drones generated RMB 1.02 billion in 2025, or 87.6% of XAG’s revenue. Agricultural rovers and autopilot systems each contributed about 1.5%, while smart-farm IoT products accounted for 3.1%.

Why automate more of the farm?

Agriculture is a difficult environment for robots. Weather and terrain change, while machines must deal with dust, water, chemicals, trees and other obstacles. A breakdown during a short spraying or planting window can quickly become costly.

Yet those constraints also strengthen the case for automation, particularly where farm labor is scarce.

In 2022, Gong told TechNode that agricultural technology would only become commercially meaningful when it could replace most of the human work in a complete production step or deliver a substantial efficiency gain. Four years later, the X Series partly reflects that vision: beyond autonomous flight, it automates charging, mixing, and refilling, reducing some of the labor still required between missions.

The global test

XAG now has to make that automation model work across very different farming systems.

According to latest Hong Kong listing filing, its distributors cover nearly 70 countries and regions. Overseas revenue reached RMB 419 million in 2025, or 35.9% of total revenue, up 13% from a year earlier.

The company is also pushing further into the U.S. In February, XAG introduced the P150 Max at the Spray Drone End User Conference in Kansas City, positioning it for spraying, spreading, mapping and on-farm logistics.

The U.S. is a useful test for XAG, where it competes with both farm-machinery incumbents and domestic drone makers. XAG enters the market with a portfolio spanning drones, smaller ground robots, and farm automation systems.

That makes XAG’s overseas expansion a test not just of its drones, but of its broader automation model. The company has already built a sizable business in the air. Its next bet is on how much work can be taken off the ground.

DragonLab cuts through the noise to find the Chinese startups, founders, and technologies that could shape what comes next.

Have a startup we should know about? Reach us at dragonlab@technode.com.

item.title: Huawei launches Mate 90 series with new Kirin chips across the lineup
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: Huawei today held its autumn product launch event in Shanghai, unveiling the Mate 90 series. The series includes five models: the Mate 90, Mate 90 Pro, Mate 90 Pro Max, Mate 90 Pro Max Collector’s Edition, and Mate 90 RS Ultimate Design. Prices range from RMB 5,999 ($895) to RMB 12,999 ($1,939). The main upgrades […]
item.content:encoded:
Huawei today held its autumn product launch event in Shanghai, unveiling the Mate 90 series. The series includes five models: the Mate 90, Mate 90 Pro, Mate 90 Pro Max, Mate 90 Pro Max Collector’s Edition, and Mate 90 RS Ultimate Design. Prices range from RMB 5,999 ($895) to RMB 12,999 ($1,939).

The main upgrades in the Mate 90 series focus on the chip, display, camera system, connectivity, and on-device AI. The new generation of Kirin chips across the lineup was one of the key highlights of the launch.

New-generation Kirin chips across the lineup

The Mate 90 is powered by the Kirin 9030. According to Huawei, its overall performance is 27% higher than that of the previous-generation Mate 80.

The Mate 90 Pro uses the Kirin 9035, which Huawei says focuses on balancing performance and power consumption. Its overall battery life has improved by 18% compared with the previous generation, according to the company.

The higher-end Mate 90 Pro Max and above are powered by the Kirin 9050 Pro. According to Huawei, the chip uses a new logical folding architecture with 5 million signal transmission bonds and achieves an inter-die bandwidth of 125 TB per second. Huawei says overall device performance is 31% higher than the previous generation, while on-device AI computing performance has doubled.

The different Kirin chips allow Huawei to maintain performance differences between the various Mate 90 models.

Display and device protection

On the display side, the Mate 90 Pro and higher-end models feature second-generation Linglong displays, with peak brightness reaching up to 12,000 nits at 1% APL.

The Mate 90 Pro Max and RS Ultimate Design further feature full-color Linglong displays with support for BT.2020 full-chain color reproduction. For general users, this mainly relates to brightness and color performance, while content creators gain additional display capabilities aimed at more professional use.

For device protection, the entire lineup uses third-generation Xuanwu strengthened Kunlun Glass, while the Pro and higher-end models use optical Kunlun Glass for the camera cover. Huawei says the overall drop resistance of the devices has improved by 20 times compared with the previous generation.

All models also support IP68 dust and water resistance, while the Pro and higher-end models add IP69 protection against high-temperature, high-pressure water jets.

Camera upgrades focus on color, dynamic range and telephoto

For imaging, the entire Mate 90 series features a third-generation Red Maple primary-color camera system and infrared optical coatings across the full focal range. Huawei says global color accuracy has improved by 37%, while skin-tone reproduction accuracy in portrait photography has improved by 62%.

The Mate 90 Pro Max takes the camera system further with an 18-stop high-dynamic-range main camera and a 200-megapixel large-sensor telephoto camera. Its stabilization is rated at CIPA 7.5. Huawei says the system has been further optimized for image stability and clarity at 20x zoom, while also improving noise control in low-light conditions.

These upgrades target several areas that have become key points of competition in smartphone imaging, including color reproduction, dynamic range, telephoto performance, and image stabilization.

On-device AI becomes another focus

For connectivity, the Mate 90 series uses a Wi-Fi and cellular integrated antenna architecture. Huawei says the design can increase signal strength by 2 dB and improve connection stability in complex environments. The Mate 90 Pro Max also supports four SIM cards with three active simultaneously.

On the AI side, the Mate 90 Pro Max and higher-end models feature a 30-billion-parameter MoE multimodal on-device model, along with functions such as Xiaoyi Call 2.0, Xiaoyi Gallery Assistant, and Xiaoyi Navigation Bar.

Compared with AI services that rely primarily on cloud computing, on-device models allow some tasks to be processed directly on the smartphone without requiring a continuous network connection. However, the actual experience will depend on the capabilities of individual models, response times, and specific usage scenarios.

The move toward larger on-device models

The Mate 90 series continues Huawei’s multi-model strategy, using differences in chips, displays, and camera systems to cover a range of price segments.

Compared with simply adding hardware specifications, a more notable change in this generation is the combination of the new chips with on-device AI. As large language models increasingly move onto smartphones, phone makers are shifting from simply offering AI-powered applications toward deploying larger models directly on devices.

Whether these hardware and AI upgrades translate into meaningful improvements in everyday use will ultimately depend on hands-on experience and longer-term testing.

item.title: BYD plans overseas launch event for Yangwang luxury brand
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: BYD plans to hold an overseas launch event for its Yangwang luxury vehicle brand, the company said in a record of its September 29 shareholder meeting. It did not give a date or location for the event. The company also said it expects its Brazil plant to produce about 250,000 vehicles this year and its […]
item.content:encoded:
BYD plans to hold an overseas launch event for its Yangwang luxury vehicle brand, the company said in a record of its September 29 shareholder meeting. It did not give a date or location for the event.

The company also said it expects its Brazil plant to produce about 250,000 vehicles this year and its Hungary plant to begin production soon. The Yangwang event would form part of BYD’s broader effort to build its premium brands outside China. [CFi, in Chinese]

item.content:encoded:
ByteDance is reportedly testing a personal AI assistant tied to Doubao and plans to release it as a standalone app. The product has been given the tentative Chinese name Xiaodou (小豆), according to a report cited by IT Home.

The app remains in internal testing, and its public name and features may change before launch. Earlier reports said the project, previously known internally as “Spell,” was being developed by the team behind the Doubao phone assistant. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed

Enterprise customers can count use of the Chinese model against their existing OpenAI spending commitments. Sina Finance described this as the first time a Chinese open model has entered OpenAI’s enterprise billing system. The arrangement lets customers use Kimi K3 […]
item.content:encoded:
Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 is entering OpenAI’s enterprise Codex channel through US inference provider Baseten. Enterprise customers can count use of the Chinese model against their existing OpenAI spending commitments. Sina Finance described this as the first time a Chinese open model has entered OpenAI’s enterprise billing system.

The arrangement lets customers use Kimi K3 within an existing procurement agreement, without adding a separate supplier contract. Baseten provides the model inference, while Codex provides the developer interface. [Sina Finance, in Chinese]

item.content:encoded:
Meituan made LongCat-2.5-Preview available through its API platform on September 25, adding image understanding to the company’s AI model lineup. The new model can answer questions about images, summarize visual content and handle more complex visual reasoning tasks, according to its documentation.

Meituan also says the model improves coding performance and works with developer tools including Claude Code, OpenCode and OpenClaw. [LongCat]

item.content:encoded:
AITO opened presales for the updated M8 SUV on September 30, with prices starting at RMB 389,800 ($54,700). The new model comes with Huawei’s ADS 5 driver-assistance system and a vehicle architecture designed with future Level 3 automated driving in mind.

The M8 remains available in battery-electric and range-extended versions. Depending on configuration, the electric model offers up to 830 kilometers of CLTC-rated range, while the range-extended version offers up to 1,435 kilometers of combined range. [Autohome, in Chinese]

item.content:encoded:
Ant Group’s InclusionAI has launched Ling-3.1-flash, a language model with 560 billion total parameters and about 25 billion activated for each token. The company is positioning it for agent tasks, search, office software and specialist applications.

The model is designed for a context window of up to one million tokens, but its current two-week free trial is limited to 256,000 tokens. InclusionAI plans to enable the larger window and release the model as open source after the trial. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: The Man Who Built China’s Screen Giant Is Betting on RISC-V
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication. Wang Dongsheng has already spent one career proving that a Chinese company could compete in one of the technology industry’s most capital-intensive businesses. In 1993, he led the creation of BOE, the display manufacturer that would grow into one of the world’s largest […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication.

Wang Dongsheng has already spent one career proving that a Chinese company could compete in one of the technology industry’s most capital-intensive businesses.

In 1993, he led the creation of BOE, the display manufacturer that would grow into one of the world’s largest producers of screens. BOE supplied the panels through which hundreds of millions of people encountered televisions, laptops and smartphones—even when they never saw its name.

Wang left the company’s chairmanship in 2019. At 62, an age when many founders would have stepped away from industrial risk, he started again.

His second act is ESWIN Computing, a Beijing chip company organized around RISC-V, the open instruction-set architecture attracting developers across embedded devices, automobiles, robotics and artificial intelligence. ESWIN is now preparing to list in Hong Kong, offering 1.57 billion H shares at between HK$1.48 and HK$1.59 each. Trading is expected to begin on October 9 under stock code 1256, according to its prospectus.

The comparison with BOE is tempting. Both companies emerged from moments when Chinese manufacturers wanted more control over a foundational layer of the electronics industry. Both required large, sustained investment before scale could improve their economics. Both were shaped by Wang’s belief that an industrial platform matters more than a single product.

But ESWIN is not yet the BOE of RISC-V. Most of its revenue still comes from chips that manage displays and touch interactions. It remains heavily lossmaking, depends on a small group of customers and is attempting to expand into several difficult markets at once.

That tension makes the company more interesting than its listing labels suggest. ESWIN’s Hong Kong offering is not simply a bet on an open chip architecture. It is a test of whether expertise accumulated around screens can become the foundation for a broader computing business—and whether Wang can repeat the logic of his first industrial transformation in a much less forgiving market.

The Industrialist Behind the Screen

To understand ESWIN, it helps to understand what Wang built before it.

BOE was founded in Beijing in 1993, when China’s electronics industry remained dependent on imported display technology and manufacturing equipment. Wang served as chairman and chief executive from the company’s creation until 2016, then remained chairman until his term ended in June 2019.

Display manufacturing is a business of scale, precision and punishing capital expenditure. A new production line can cost billions of dollars. Technical generations turn over quickly, and the value of a panel tends to decline as manufacturing improves. Competitors must finance the next factory before the previous one has fully paid for itself.

BOE survived that cycle and became a global display supplier. The experience appears to have shaped Wang’s view of technology companies: individual components matter, but the deeper objective is to assemble talent, intellectual property, manufacturing relationships and customers into a platform capable of surviving several product generations.

ESWIN Group was created in 2019 around that platform idea. Its semiconductor activities were separated into businesses covering chip products, 12-inch silicon wafers, board-level packaging and testing, and display-driver packaging and testing. ESWIN Computing took the chip-product business that had begun operating under a predecessor organization in 2018.

This distinction is important. ESWIN Computing does not manufacture wafers or package every chip it sells. It operates largely as a fabless company: it researches and designs chips, chipsets and circuit boards, develops the software required to use them, and relies on third parties for fabrication, packaging and testing.

The company was formally established in Beijing in September 2019. It also created a central research institute to work on RISC-V computing architecture, high-speed interfaces and reusable intellectual-property modules. Wang initially served as chairman. Mi Peng, who joined as chief financial officer in 2019, is now chairman and chief executive, while Wang remains an executive director and chairs the strategy and investment committee.

Other senior figures point to the kind of organization ESWIN wanted to build. Vice chairman Wang Bo spent almost 24 years at Intel, most recently as a product director. The broader technical team includes veterans of chip design, displays, connectivity and computing.

Rather than begin with one flagship processor, ESWIN accumulated a library. As of March 2026, it reported more than 620 IP modules, over 20 series of RISC-V cores and more than 1,740 patent applications incorporated across its products. It had commercialized over 150 hardware-software products and served 220 customers during the reporting period covered by its prospectus.

This breadth is both the company’s proposition and its first complication.

What RISC-V Actually Opens

RISC-V—pronounced “risk five”—is not a chip. It is an instruction-set architecture, or ISA: the basic vocabulary and rules that allow software to tell a processor what to do.

For decades, most personal computers and data-center processors have been built around the x86 instruction sets associated with Intel and AMD, while smartphones and countless embedded devices rely on architectures licensed from Arm. Chip designers can build their own processors around those systems, but they operate within commercially controlled ecosystems.

RISC-V is an open, royalty-free standard. Its core specifications can be used by companies, universities and developers to design processors without paying for the instruction set itself. The architecture is modular, allowing designers to begin with a relatively small base and add capabilities required for a specific product.

Open does not mean that every RISC-V chip must be open source. A company can use the public instruction set while keeping its processor design, specialized modules and software proprietary. The value of the standard is that it gives designers more freedom to customize hardware without abandoning a common software target.

That makes RISC-V particularly attractive for devices that sit outside the conventional PC and smartphone categories. A car controller, industrial sensor, storage appliance or robot may need a different balance of performance, power consumption, cost and real-time responsiveness. Developers can tailor a processor around those needs while reusing tools and software developed across the wider RISC-V ecosystem.

The difficult part is everything beyond the specification. A commercially useful chip needs verified processor cores, interfaces, compilers, operating systems, development tools, application software, documentation and engineers who can help customers integrate it. An architecture becomes powerful only when enough of that surrounding ecosystem exists.

ESWIN is trying to occupy the layer between the open standard and the finished device. It develops RISC-V cores and reusable IP, combines them with other processing and connectivity functions, packages those elements into chips or boards, and supplies the software required to make them work in particular applications.

The company calls its development environment RISAA. The platform is designed to let teams reuse hardware and software modules rather than begin each product from zero. ESWIN can sell finished products, customize them for major customers or license individual IP blocks to companies developing their own chips.

In theory, this creates a compounding advantage. Each project adds technology that can be reused in the next one, reducing development time and spreading research costs across a larger range of products. In practice, the benefits arrive only if enough customers choose the platform—and if the company can prevent its product range from becoming an expensive collection of unrelated projects.

The Display Business Paying for the Future

Despite its RISC-V positioning, ESWIN’s present business remains closely connected to Wang’s previous industry.

The company’s largest product group consists of human-machine interaction chips. These components sit inside televisions, monitors, laptops, smartphones and watches. Timing controllers organize the flow of image data toward a display. Touch controllers translate a finger’s movement into commands. Other chips manage power or help display drivers turn electronic signals into visible pixels.

These are rarely the parts advertised to consumers, but a screen cannot function without them. The display supply chain also gave ESWIN a ready set of engineering problems and customer relationships. In 2025, the company was China’s largest domestic provider of human-machine interaction chips for smart devices by revenue, according to market research commissioned for the prospectus.

Human-machine interaction products generated RMB1.86 billion in 2025, or 76.3% of ESWIN’s total revenue. Multimedia-processing chips—including television system-on-chips, monitor scalers and Mini-LED or Micro-LED controllers—added another 6.2%.

Together, screen-related products accounted for more than four-fifths of the business. They are not a historical footnote. They are the revenue base supporting ESWIN’s expansion.

The company has continued to develop that base. In 2025, a leading monitor manufacturer began mass production of a RISC-V multimedia controller supplied by ESWIN. Its OLED display-driver chip was adopted by a leading smartphone manufacturer. These products show how RISC-V can be introduced inside familiar devices, often in control functions invisible to the user.

They also reveal the limit of describing ESWIN as a computing startup. Its commercial strength was built around displays, an industry in which Wang already understood the technology, customers and supply chain. The more ambitious parts of the story are newer.

From Screens to Machines That Act

ESWIN divides its growth products into interconnectivity and computing.

Interconnectivity products allow vehicles, robots and industrial equipment to transmit and receive data through Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular networks. Computing products range from microcontrollers that manage a limited set of operations to AI systems-on-chips capable of processing sensor data and making decisions locally.

The company groups these markets under “embodied intelligence,” an industry term for machines that sense and act in the physical world. In practical terms, this includes cars coordinating electronic systems, robots interpreting their surroundings and industrial equipment responding to real-time conditions.

ESWIN began emphasizing edge and automotive products in 2021. It delivered its first 32-bit RISC-V IP that year and a 64-bit version in 2023. Its automotive development program followed in 2022. By 2025, a RISC-V microcontroller had entered mass production with an automotive-parts supplier and a vehicle manufacturer.

The company has moved further into computing through boards and systems. Its products now span edge-computing chips, multi-purpose computing hardware and video-transcoding cards. In 2026, it began developing a high-performance RISC-V AI system-on-chip for large-model inference. Another RISC-V AI chip was adopted by a consumer-storage manufacturer for personal-storage products.

The financial statements suggest that this activity is beginning to matter. Computing products generated only RMB375,000 in 2023. Revenue rose to RMB72.3 million in 2024 and RMB319.8 million in 2025, reaching 13.2% of the company total.

During the first three months of 2026, computing revenue reached RMB223 million, almost half of quarterly sales. That number should be treated carefully: large system projects can make one quarter look very different from the next. It nevertheless shows why ESWIN wants investors to view it as more than a display-chip supplier.

The transition is not a conventional pivot. ESWIN has not abandoned screens to chase AI. It is attempting to reuse the same platform—processor cores, interfaces, software and supply-chain relationships—across devices that require more connectivity and local computing.

The question is whether that reuse is technically and economically real. A timing controller for a monitor, an automotive microcontroller and an inference chip operate under very different requirements. Shared architecture can lower part of the development burden, but every market still demands specialized engineering, qualification and customer support.

The Cost of Building Before Scale

ESWIN’s revenue has grown steadily. It rose from RMB1.75 billion in 2023 to RMB2.03 billion in 2024 and RMB2.43 billion in 2025. Gross margin improved from 15.4% to 18.6% over the same period.

The company remains far from profitable.

ESWIN lost RMB1.84 billion in 2023, RMB1.55 billion in 2024 and RMB1.52 billion in 2025. It lost a further RMB374.9 million during the first quarter of 2026 and says it expects losses to continue for the foreseeable future.

Research and development explains much of the gap. R&D expense reached RMB1.44 billion in 2023—more than 80% of revenue that year—and remained above RMB1 billion in 2025. Administrative and sales expenses add another layer of cost, while new products require investment long before they produce meaningful volume.

This is where comparisons with BOE become useful and dangerous at the same time. Both displays and chips reward patient investment, but they scale differently. A panel factory can produce large volumes of relatively standardized output once capacity is installed. A chip-platform company must repeatedly persuade customers to design its technology into products, then maintain software and engineering support across many applications.

ESWIN argues that reuse will gradually improve the economics. Once a processor core, interface or software module has been developed and verified, it can be incorporated into several products. Higher shipment volumes can spread tape-out, software and support costs across more units. Customized projects can also create reusable modules for later customers.

There are signs of improvement. Adjusted net loss narrowed from RMB1.70 billion in 2023 to RMB1.16 billion in 2025, after excluding share-based payments and listing expenses. Gross profit rose each year. But ESWIN is still spending ahead of the scale required to support its platform.

The Hong Kong offering will extend that runway. At the midpoint of its price range, the company expects approximately HK$2.27 billion in net proceeds. It plans to allocate 35% to developing and updating chip products, 30% to the RISAA hardware-software platform, 15% to potential acquisitions, 10% to marketing and the RISC-V ecosystem, and 10% to working capital.

That allocation makes the purpose of the listing unusually clear: investors are being asked to finance more platform before the existing platform has reached profitability.

The Customer Behind the Concentration

ESWIN’s revenue base is not only concentrated by product. It is concentrated by customer.

The five largest customers generated 89.5% of revenue in 2025. The largest alone contributed 64.6%, although that was down from 82.1% in 2023. During the first quarter of 2026, the largest customer’s share fell to 39.3% as computing revenue expanded.

Such concentration is common when a young chip supplier wins a high-volume design with a major electronics manufacturer. It can accelerate growth because one successful product reaches millions of devices. It also gives the customer significant influence over pricing, inventory and the timing of orders.

ESWIN’s prospectus does not identify its largest customer by name. It describes the company as a Shenzhen-listed provider of intelligent interface products and professional services that buys mainly human-machine interaction chips for televisions, monitors and smartphones.

The relationship places ESWIN’s BOE heritage in the background even when the customer remains anonymous. Wang’s industry experience made it possible to begin with a market the company understood. The long-term test is whether ESWIN can build a customer base that no longer depends so heavily on any one display ecosystem.

Inventory creates a related risk. Net inventory rose from RMB328.6 million at the end of 2023 to RMB780.1 million by March 2026 as the company prepared for new products and anticipated demand. Earlier-generation connectivity products had already required substantial write-downs. In chips, preparing too little inventory can mean missing a customer launch; preparing too much can leave expensive components obsolete.

The platform strategy is meant to diversify both products and customers. It will succeed only if the newer automotive, robotics, industrial and computing products move from technical milestones into repeatable sales.

A Second Industrial Bet

Wang Dongsheng’s first major company helped shift the geography of display manufacturing. ESWIN is attempting something less visible and potentially broader: building reusable computing technology that can appear inside many categories of machines.

RISC-V gives the company an opening. The architecture lowers one barrier to processor design and offers customers an alternative to proprietary instruction sets. It does not remove the harder barriers—software, verification, manufacturing, customer trust and the enormous cost of sustaining a product roadmap.

ESWIN has assembled many of the necessary pieces. It has commercial products, large customers, processor cores, a growing IP library and a founder who has already endured one long industrial cycle. Its display business provides revenue and a route into high-volume devices. Its computing products are beginning to change the mix.

It also has the profile of a company still proving the central claim behind its existence. Revenue remains dominated by screen-related chips. Losses remain large. Customer concentration remains high. AI inference, robotics and automotive computing are promising markets, but they are also crowded with established chipmakers and heavily funded startups.

The Hong Kong listing does not resolve those contradictions. It gives ESWIN more time and capital to work through them.

That may be the most revealing connection between Wang’s two companies. BOE was not built through a single technological breakthrough; it was built through repeated investment, manufacturing discipline and the willingness to remain in a difficult industry long enough for scale to matter.

ESWIN is now making a similar argument about computing platforms. The difference is that an open architecture allows many companies to start. Only a few will build enough technology around it to make customers stay.

item.title: ByteDance’s Doubao reportedly preparing personal AI agent, codenamed Spell and tested since April

item.content:encoded:
ByteDance’s AI assistant Doubao is reportedly accelerating work on a new personal AI agent. According to sources, the project began internal testing as early as April and was previously known internally as Spell. Product development has recently picked up pace, with a public launch expected in the near future.

The move could mark a shift in Doubao’s evolution from an AI chatbot toward a more autonomous agent that can handle tasks on behalf of users, rather than simply responding to prompts.

Internally tested since April, initially developed by the Doubao Phone Assistant team

According to Sina Tech, Spell was initially led by the Doubao Phone Assistant team and entered small-scale internal testing in April. The core idea was to move AI beyond simply answering questions and toward actually completing tasks on behalf of users, an approach increasingly described in the industry as a Personal Agent.

The project had not previously been disclosed publicly. One factor was the development timeline of Doubao’s phone assistant, while the broader concept of personal AI agents was still at a relatively early stage.

That appears to be changing. As products such as Meta Muse and OpenAI’s “o” have attracted growing attention overseas, Personal Agents are moving from an emerging concept toward a product category that major AI companies are increasingly competing in. This has also prompted Doubao to accelerate development of its own personal AI agent.

Spell’s technology is now being folded into Doubao

The new product is not being built entirely from scratch. Sources said Doubao is now integrating the technical capabilities developed through the original Spell project with core capabilities from the Doubao conversational AI team. The two teams are expected to jointly work on further product development and launch.

Looking at the bigger picture, the project can be seen as an extension of Doubao’s technical work on mobile AI agents over the past two years.

In December 2025, Doubao first unveiled a technical preview of its phone assistant. A consumer version followed in September this year. After multiple rounds of validation in mobile scenarios, Doubao is now looking to extend those agent capabilities from a phone assistant into a more general-purpose personal assistant.

The phone assistant may have been just the starting point. Personal Agent could be the next direction Doubao is exploring.

Doubao is building out its agent portfolio

Doubao has already been expanding its presence in the Agent space. On August 25, it launched Doubao Work, an Agent product designed for enterprise and office scenarios. It can handle tasks ranging from drafting documents and organizing meeting notes to processing data across different software tools.

The company has since added features including editing of local Office files, task handoffs across up to five devices, and the ability to create customized skills through screen recordings.

The overall direction is becoming increasingly clear: for businesses, AI can help you get work done. For consumers, it could help manage everyday tasks and personal affairs. If the personal AI agent launches as expected, Doubao would effectively be pursuing two parallel agent tracks: enterprise applications and consumer use.

AI agents are moving from chatting to doing

Over the past two years, AI competition has largely focused on model capabilities, reasoning and generation quality. But as AI agents evolve, the focus is shifting from answering questions to getting things done.

Users increasingly want AI that can remember preferences, understand goals and complete tasks on their behalf, from gathering information and handling software to organizing content and executing workflows.

That is where Doubao’s potential personal assistant fits in. Rather than simply adding another chatbot, it could extend Doubao’s existing agent capabilities into a broader personal AI assistant for everyday use. How far it can go, however, will only become clear after the product launches.
